questiontext.text:
A survey is conducted in four out of ten of these villages shown below.

The aim of the survey is to determine variables that affect the yield of rice. There are six other variables in the resulting data set from the survey: village, field, size, fertiliser, fertiliser group and variety.

  • Village is the village where the survey was performed.
  • Field is the field within a village where the crop was grown.
  • Size is a measurement of the field size in acres.
  • Fertiliser is the fertiliser amount. This is a numerical variable.
  • Fertiliser Group is the fertiliser variable categorised as a factor.
  • Variety is the type of variety of rice - there are three varieties: Old, New, and Traditional.


Here we work through some questions to illustrate unbalanced data.


1. Fit a pivot table containing Village and Fertiliser Group, looking at the frequency sizes for each group. Would you say this data is balanced?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

[[feedback:prt1]]


2.   (a) Which village accounts for the highest yield?

[[input:ans2a]] [[validation:ans2a]]

(b) Which fertiliser group accounts for the highest yield?

[[input:ans2b]] [[validation:ans2b]]

[[feedback:prt2]]


3. An ANOVA table divides the variability into the part that is accounted for, and the residual. When the residual variability – the part that is not accounted for – is low, then the information from the data becomes clear. In the ANOVA table, the mean squares are roughly variances (a common measure of variation).

[[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]

[[feedback:prt3]]


4. Add fertiliser to the model, with village fitted before fertiliser. Now what variation does the village account for in the data?

[[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]]

[[feedback:prt4]]


5. Switch around the two explanatory variables, fitting fertiliser before village. Now what variation does the village account for in the data?

[[input:ans5]] [[validation:ans5]]

[[feedback:prt5]]

truefeedback.text:
Great! We can see that the data is unbalanced by a simple frequency table. Here we have the villages as rows, and the fertiliser level as columns.

Low Medium High Total
Sabey 1 3 6 10
Kesen 3 2 2 7
Niko 4 1 0 5
Nanda 1 4 9 14
Total 9 10 17 36

Looking at this table, it is clear that the group sizes vary between fertiliser group and village; a higher fertiliser is used frequently in Nanda, but is never used in the Niko village. This unbalanced data leads to the question: is the variability in the yield because of a higher fertiliser, or because they’re in that village?

An investigation into the data can help clarify the answer. We can look at the mean yield by village, and the mean yield by fertiliser group.

truefeedback.text:
We can see that Sabey accounts for the highest yield.
We can see that the villages vary in mean yield between them.

Village Mean yield
Sabey 45.33
Kesen 32.76
Niko 30.56
Nanda 44.68

We can also see that the highest fertiliser level results in the largest yield on average, and the lowest fertiliser level results in the smallest average yield.

Comparing the mean yields with the table of frequencies, we can see that villages that use the high fertiliser level more often result in a higher mean yield. In Sabey, 6 of 10 fertiliser levels are high, and in Nanda it is 9 of 14. Could this explain why Sabey and Nanda had high yields?

Low Medium High Total
Sabey 1 3 6 10
Kesen 3 2 2 7
Niko 4 1 0 5
Nanda 1 4 9 14
Total 9 10 17 36

Hence, in this data set, the variation between the villages can be explained by village or the fertiliser level.

Fertiliser Level Mean yield
Low 27.42
Medium 37.69
High 49.25

You are correct that Sabey has the highest yield on average.
However, the fertiliser group is incorrect. Try again.

Try with PivotTables, using the Fertiliser Level as a Column or Row, and setting Yield as the Value. Make sure you change the Value Field Settings to be mean.

You are correct that the “High” fertiliser resulting in the highest yield on average.
However, the village is incorrect. Try again.

Try with PivotTables, using the Village as a Column or Row, and setting Yield as the Value. Make sure you change the Value Field Settings to be mean.

truefeedback.text:
The variation is the Mean Squared Error for Village. If just village is fitted, the village is found to significantly affect the outcome variable. The variation between the villages is quite large, 464, compared with the residual value of 111.

Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr (>F)
Village 3 1391.2 463.73 4.1642 0.01343
Residuals 32 3563.6 111.36

It looks as if you’ve fitted the correct model but responded with the wrong value from the table.
The variation is the “Mean Squared Error” for Village.

falsefeedback.text:
Not quite.
See here for information on fitting an ANOVA in Excel.

truefeedback.text:
If we then add fertiliser to the model, then more of the variability is accounted for, from both the village and fertiliser variables.

Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr (>F)
Village 3 1391 464 7.37 0.00077
Fertiliser 2 1675 837 13.30 7.3e-05
Residuals 30 1889 63

It looks as if you’ve fitted the correct model but responded with the wrong value from the table.
The variation is the “Mean Squared Error” for Village.

falsefeedback.text:
Not quite.
See here for information on fitting an ANOVA in Excel.

truefeedback.text:
If instead, fertiliser is fitted before village, the fertiliser is found to affect the outcome variable, and village does not.

Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr (>F)
Fertiliser 2 2919 1459 23.18 8.2e-07
Village 3 147 49 0.78 0.51
Residuals 30 1889 63

Hence, the order that village and variable are inputted into the model changes the model itself. The reason for this is that the data is unbalanced.

This is because in some villages, a higher proportion of those surveyed use high fertiliser. Hence, it looks like village has an effect when fertiliser is omitted from the model, when actually it is fertiliser.

Note that we are lucky. In other data sets, the variation could be down to a variable that isn't measured in the data set, such as the soil type or the climate!
